sections.0.body.0.t: DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) tests the running application from the outside in, as a black box: the scanner sends malicious requests and observes the responses, as an attacker would, without access to the source code.

sections.0.body.1.t: Because it operates on the real, assembled system, DAST validates what SAST does not see: server configuration, HTTP headers, authentication, session and the interaction between components.

sections.1.bullets.0.t: crawling: a spider maps the application's endpoints, forms and parameters

sections.1.bullets.1.t: fuzzing: every discovered input receives attack payloads (SQLi, XSS, path traversal, SSRF)

sections.1.bullets.2.t: response analysis: the scanner checks whether the attack was reflected, executed or leaked information

sections.1.bullets.3.t: passive checks: missing headers, cookies without flags, exposed versions

sections.2.body.0.t: The scanner found an id parameter in the crawler. First step: the classic SQL injection test, closing the quote and inserting an always-true condition. What the scanner sends:

sections.3.body.0.t: The SQLi signature is in the response: instead of one user, all of them came back, because the injected condition became part of the query. The scanner compares this response with the baseline of the original parameter and concludes: injectable.

sections.4.body.0.t: The response does not always return the data, and modern engines hide the error. For these cases, the scanner uses blind injections and infers from behavior. A controlled delay is the evidence:

sections.4.code.0.code.t:
GET /users?id=1'%20AND%20SLEEP(5)--  HTTP/1.1

with the payload:     response in 5.2 s
without the payload:  response in 0.1 s
                  => the database ran the SLEEP: blind injectable

sections.4.heading.t: When there is no echo: blind injection

sections.5.body.0.t: After deploying to staging or preview: the pipeline brings up the environment and points the scanner at it, failing on critical findings. Scheduled scans against production cover what changes outside the release cycle.

sections.5.heading.t: Where it fits in the pipeline

sections.6.bullets.0.t: strength: reports what is actually exploitable, with a very low false positive rate, because it only asserts what it triggered

sections.6.bullets.1.t: strength: language-agnostic, since it tests HTTP, not code

sections.6.bullets.2.t: weakness: only sees the exposed surface; code without a reachable route is left out

sections.6.bullets.3.t: weakness: slow and late, finding issues after deploy, when fixing is already costly

short.t: Dynamic testing of the running application

tagline.t: Attacks the running application the way a malicious user would, without seeing the code.
